Anchor Retail Group - Q2 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Anchor Retail Group Q2 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, during the Q&A session, please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Anchor Retail Group's results for the second quarter of fiscal 2024. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report Anchor Retail Group's performance for the second quarter of fiscal 2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover four key aspects of our performance:

1. **Sales per Square Foot:** We achieved company-wide sales per square foot of $428, reflecting a 4.2% increase year-over-year and our 11th straight quarter of gains, positioning us strongly among department store peers.

2. **Traffic vs. Ticket Breakdown:** Our comparable store sales grew 2.8%, driven by a slight dip in traffic offset by stronger average ticket sizes, highlighting our focus on higher-value transactions.

3. **Store Remodel and Renovation Plans:** We're ramping up investments in our NextGen store prototypes, targeting 250 remodels this fiscal year to boost comps and efficiency.

4. **Marketing Initiatives:** Marketing spend rose to support our omnichannel push, with digital channels leading the way for better returns on ad spend.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the second quarter of fiscal 2024.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $1.34 billion, a 5.2% increase compared to the same period last year, fueled by strength across our core divisions and resilient consumer demand in key categories.

Gross margin expanded to 38.5%, up 120 basis points year-over-year, primarily driven by a favorable product mix shift toward higher-margin beauty and premium apparel collaborations, coupled with ongoing shrink mitigation efforts.

Operating expenses were $450 million, representing 33.6% of revenue, as we balanced investments in growth areas with disciplined cost controls.

Net income came in at $85.2 million, translating to diluted earnings per share of $1.25.

We generated $145 million in cash flow from operations, supporting our capital allocation priorities.

Inventory levels are currently well-controlled at $850 million, down 3% from last year, reflecting improved turns and targeted reductions in slower-moving SKUs.

Now, let me expand on some of these drivers, starting with one of our core productivity metrics: sales per square foot, or SPSF. For context, we calculate SPSF as total net sales divided by our average selling square footage, excluding non-revenue areas like backrooms and offices. This metric is crucial for gauging space efficiency in retail, particularly with escalating real estate expenses and the ongoing shift toward e-commerce. In Q2, our company-wide SPSF hit $428, up 4.2% from $411 a year ago, landing us at the upper end of department store peers—surpassing Macy's recent $390 figure and approaching specialty players like TJX's $500-plus in off-price setups.

Breaking it down by segment, our Apparel & Accessories division, which makes up 52% of selling space, delivered $465 SPSF, a 6.1% year-over-year rise. This stemmed from an enriched assortment, with average unit retail climbing 3.8% to $52.45, boosted by exclusive partnerships such as our Levi's vintage collection and athleisure lines inspired by Lululemon collaborators. Units per transaction also rose 2.7% to 2.4, aided by bundled "Shop the Look" displays in prime areas. In Home & Lifestyle, comprising 28% of space, SPSF reached $372, up 2.9%, thanks to engaging setups like immersive kitchen displays featuring Sub-Zero-style appliances, which improved conversion by 1.5 points to 28%.

Beauty & Fragrance, at 12% of space, shone brightest with $612 SPSF, surging 8.4% year-over-year, echoing Ulta's category strength through shop-in-shops with Fenty-level brands and our clean beauty exclusives, which posted 22% comparable growth. Footwear & Accessories lagged slightly at $389, up 1.8%, impacted by milder winter weather curbing outerwear sales.

This quarter's results build on a multi-year recovery; SPSF troughed at $362 in FY2021 during COVID disruptions, with 18% cumulative growth since then, outperforming the NRF retail productivity index by 5 points. Comparable store sales added 3.8 points via 1.2% traffic growth and stable 26% conversion, while the balance came from space reallocations and new formats. Shrink improved 40 basis points to 1.4%, driven by RFID implementation across 85% of our 1,200 stores, similar to advanced tagging systems we've studied.

Geographically, Northeast urban hubs—New York, Chicago, Boston—led with $482 SPSF, up 5.7%, leveraging dense mall traffic in Simon Property centers; our Herald Square flagship exceeded $1,200, on par with top Nordstrom locations. Sunbelt regions like Florida, Texas, and Arizona followed at $445, up 6.3%, boosted by migration and tourism, including optimized prototypes in Miami's Brickell City Centre with 70% open selling space. Midwest and rural areas trailed at $395, up only 1.1%, hit by weather and value competition from Ross Stores; we're countering with "right-sizing," converting 20 big-box stores over 100,000 square feet to 40,000-square-foot express formats projecting $550-plus SPSF.

Key enablers include our Omnichannel Lab in 40 stores, where BOPIS zones—5% of space—generate 15% of sales, lifting SPSF 7-9 points. RFID and AI planograms cut out-of-stocks 22%, prioritizing fast-turn private-label activewear at 12x inventory turns versus the category's 8x. We've committed $250 million in CapEx this year to "3.0" prototypes with open layouts, 20% better sightlines, interactive mirrors like Neiman Marcus, and micro-fulfillment for same-day delivery, yielding 12% SPSF gains in renovated stores. We're also testing 8,000-square-foot "Anchor Pods" in strip malls at $650 SPSF, akin to Walmart neighborhood concepts.

Portfolio management remains disciplined: We've closed 15% of sub-$300 SPSF doors since 2022, redirecting capital to expansions. Our outlets, now 18% of space, hit $510 SPSF, up 7%, via "treasure hunt" mixes of excess Nike and Ralph Lauren inventory, capturing more full-price sales TJX-style.

For FY2024, we expect 4-6% SPSF growth to $440-$450. Holiday momentum could drive 8-10% comps with +3% Black Friday traffic. Risks like import tariffs on 10% of goods and mall REIT issues are mitigated by our 92% prime locations; sustained consumer sentiment above 70 on the Conference Board index supports outperformance.

Shifting to our comparable store sales drivers, let's unpack the traffic versus ticket breakdown, the bedrock of our 2.8% comp growth this quarter amid inflation, consumer confidence at 98.7 per Conference Board, and e-commerce rivalry from Amazon and Wayfair. Comps decompose into traffic times conversion times average ticket. Traffic edged down 0.4% year-over-year, more than offset by a 3.2% jump in average ticket to $128.45, aligning with our post-2022 emphasis on premium baskets.

On traffic, our 1,200 U.S. stores averaged 1.2 million weekly visitors, down 0.4% but improved from Q2's -1.1%. "Storefront Surge" geofencing via Foursquare and Google Maps boosted urban traffic 4.2%, with 15% conversion from app alerts drawing shoppers to private-label apparel and home goods. Sunbelt markets grew 1.8% traffic via 50 new formats with curbside enhancements, like Tractor Supply tactics. Midwest and Northwest fell 2.1% from weather and floods; Canada was -0.3%, while U.K. pilots gained 0.9% from "Try Before You Buy" zones.

E-commerce shift eroded 3-5% traffic per Nielsen, but BOPIS captured 22% of digital sales. For tickets, the 3.2% gain beat NRF's 2.1%, via premium shifts: big-ticket home and apparel up 7.4% units, AUR +5.1% to $450 on exclusive lines. Hardlines like bundled "Project Packs" grew tickets 4.1%; softlines flat at 0.8%. Anchor Rewards members (68% of traffic) averaged 2.3x non-member AUR, with kiosks adding $8.72 per basket. AI dynamic pricing on 18,000 SKUs via Shelfie lifted 2.7%, and 41% contactless payments cut abandonment 9%.

This marks three quarters of ticket strength (+3.0% trailing twelve months), mirroring pro segmentation at Home Depot—our pro sales at 42%, tickets $245 vs. $85 DIY. Traffic stabilized 70 basis points sequentially. FY24 CapEx includes $150 million for EV chargers and AR planners in 40% of stores, eyeing 3-5% conversion gains. Sunbelt relocations target +2% traffic; unemployment over 4.2% risks -1.5%, but 55% gross margins buffer us.

Turning to marketing and advertising expenses within SG&A, we spent $52.3 million in Q2, up 14.2% from $45.8 million, or 3.9% of sales versus 3.4%. This supports our omnichannel shift amid inflation and rates pressuring physical traffic, as seen at Target and Macy's. Digital media surged 28% to 62% of budget ($32.4 million), while traditional TV, radio, and OOH fell 8% to $19.7 million for ROI focus. Customer acquisition cost rose to $28 from $25, but lifetime value grew 11% to $420 via repeats.

This fuels "Store-to-Web" using our Customer Data Platform with Salesforce and Adobe, plus Google Cloud AI for geo-fenced promos—like kitchen lines lifting Southeast store visits 22% within 5 miles, ROAS at 4.8x beating our 3.5x threshold, akin to Home Depot. Sunbelt spend grew 9% but drove 35% more traffic via TikTok influencers and AR try-ons like IKEA. Northeast up 20% countered soft comps, ROAS 3.2x with loyalty doubles on appliances. International flat at $4.1 million (2.8% of sales) emphasized Roku shoppable TV for 15% e-com uplift.

Q3 spend grows low-teens percent of sales, tilting to retargeting private-label outdoor items versus Tractor Supply. Full-year ROI targets 10-15% gains via ML attribution across events, apps, and social, defending share against Amazon while growing experientially.

Finally, on store remodels—a top growth driver—our FY2025 CapEx is $650 million, up 20%, with $425 million (65%) for 250 remodels, up from 180, prioritizing top 40% AUV stores ($45 million vs. chain $32 million). Acceleration to 350 in FY26 hits Northeast and Sunbelt highs per Placer.ai.

The 60,000-square-foot NextGen prototype, piloted in 15 Texas/Florida stores, drove 7.2% comps, 18% dwell to 28 minutes, conversion to 41%. Features: 5,000 sq ft omnichannel hubs with 99.5% RFID accuracy via Zebra, cutting picks 40% for 85% same-day in 10 miles (omnichannel at 28%, +500 bps). AI merchandising adjusts endcaps on 15 million transactions, pairing appliances with private organics (+12% units). 20% experiential zones with demos, LED/HVAC savings (22%, $15 million rebates), slashing shrink to 1.2%. Checkout cuts 50% lanes with vision tech, NCR Voyix.

Regional: Sunbelt (40%) adds hurricane resilience for 8% pops; Northeast (25%) micro-fulfillment vs. 45% e-comm; Midwest (20%) value hardlines (+10% comps); West (15%) EV/sustainability vs. Costco.

NPV $2.5 billion, IRR 22%, three-year payback per NRF 5-8% outperformance. Fixed contracts cap inflation; H1 remodel drag 4%, +200 bps tailwind later. This offensively grabs share where physical drives 70% sales.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. As a reminder, please limit to one question and one follow-up. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of persistent inflation on your sales?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Inflation has indeed pressured value-conscious shoppers, particularly in Midwest rural areas where traffic softened, but we've offset this through premium mix shifts in beauty and apparel, higher tickets, and targeted marketing in resilient Sunbelt markets. Our private-label pricing, 30% below branded, and bundling like Project Packs have sustained comps at 2.8%, with expectations for stabilization as sentiment holds.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Rodriguez with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Rodriguez (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Emily. For Q3, we anticipate same-store sales growth of 3-5%, with upside from holiday traffic modeled at +3% and remodel tailwinds flipping positive. SPSF guides to continued 4-6% full-year progress, assuming no major macro downturns like unemployment above 4.2%.

Operator:
Our next question is from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee (Morgan Stanley):
Lisa, on the remodel program, how are you thinking about the CapEx ramp and ROI timelines given supply chain risks?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
David, great question. The $650 million FY25 CapEx is front-loaded but delivers three-year payback at 22% IRR, with pilots already showing 7.2% comp lifts and shrink down to 1.2%. We've dual-sourced semiconductors from Honeywell to mitigate delays, and fixed-price deals with suppliers like Milliken cap escalations at 3%. Early NextGen stores validate the NPV over $2.5 billion.

Operator:
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.

aspect_summary.Sales per square foot: Achieved company-wide $428 SPSF, up 4.2% YoY for 11th straight quarter; strong segment performance (Beauty $612 +8.4%, Apparel $465 +6.1%); FY2024 guide 4-6% growth to $440-$450, driven by assortments, RFID, space optimization.
aspect_summary.Marketing and advertising expense trends: Q2 spend $52.3M, up 14.2% YoY to 3.9% of sales; digital up 28% to 62% of budget, traditional down 8%; supports omnichannel with improved ROAS (4.8x), Q3 low-teens growth as % of sales.
aspect_summary.Traffic vs. Ticket breakdown analysis: Comps +2.8% from -0.4% traffic (offset by geofencing, BOPIS) and +3.2% average ticket to $128.45; driven by premium mix, loyalty (Rewards 2.3x AUR), bundling; three quarters of ticket strength.
aspect_summary.Store remodel and renovation plans: Targeting 250 NextGen remodels this FY ($425M of $650M FY2025 CapEx), up from 180; pilots yield 7.2% comps, 18% dwell time, shrink to 1.2%; features omnichannel hubs, AI, experiential zones; accelerate to 350 in FY26.
